arquitetura.texto: Fuel Mind is plain JavaScript on Firebase, with no framework and no build step. The code lives in three folders: `src/core` (Firebase, session, sync), `src/shared` (calculations and the PDF and spreadsheet template), and `src/screens`, one screen per file. `index.html` loads all scripts into the same global scope. Master data lives in `dados/compartilhado`, and each company's invoices in a document of their own, `dados/lanc__{id}`.

decisoes.texto: A Firestore rule evaluates the whole document: while all invoices lived together, anyone who could read their own could read every company's. I split the invoices into `dados/lanc__{id}`, with the company id in the name, and the rule extracts that id and checks it against the profile's `empresaIds`. Using the id, not the name, lets a company be renamed without moving the document or redoing permissions.

No freight amount is stored: the screen recalculates everything every time it opens. With the rate as a single value, changing it silently rewrote months already paid. So each change closes the previous effective period and opens a new one, and `calcularFretesDoMes` uses the rate and the driver percentage in effect on the unloading date, plus the truck combination that included that license plate on that day.

In Chrome set to Portuguese, `<input type="number">` fails silently: a comma empties the field and the mouse wheel changes the value. I replaced it with text fields, and `parseNumeroBR` interprets the number. `numerico.js` brings back the numeric keyboard on phones and the formatting, with each field's decimal places; the price accepts up to ten, the limit of `vUnCom` in the NF-e (Brazilian electronic invoice).

desafio.titulo: Admin restricted to their own companies
desafio.texto: Companies and month-end closes live in lists inside a single document, and Firestore rules can't iterate over a list. Without a limit, an admin of company A could change company B's freight rate through the console. The solution was to compare before and after with `removeAll`, which leaves only the changed items, and check each one against the profile. Since the rules have no loops, they check up to 8 changed items per write and reject any write that changes more than that.

testes.texto: The project has 120 unit tests with `node --test`, with nothing to install: they load the files in `src/` with `vm`, as the browser does. They cover freight, effective periods, the closed-month lock, matching each NF-e to the supply base that issued it, numbers, and the PDF and spreadsheet template. The security rules have 25 tests on the Firestore emulator, with a `demo-` project that doesn't exist in the cloud. GitHub Actions runs both on every push.
